seo.title: Alcohol Use Disorder Treatment in St. Louis | Plan Your Recovery
seo.description: Alcohol use disorder treatment in St. Louis — naltrexone, outpatient detox, CBT, and family therapy. Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous; we provide medically supervised detox when needed.

condition.name: Alcohol Use Disorder
condition.schemaDescription: Alcohol use disorder is a medical condition characterized by an impaired ability to stop or control alcohol use despite adverse social, occupational, or health consequences, including physical dependence and the risk of life-threatening withdrawal.

hero.headline: Alcohol Use Disorder Treatment in St. Louis
hero.intro: Alcohol use disorder is a medical condition — not a lack of willpower, not a character flaw, and not something people choose. It is the most common substance use disorder in the United States, affecting roughly 30 million people at any given time, and one of the most undertreated. It is also uniquely dangerous among substance use disorders: withdrawal from alcohol can cause seizures and death. Effective, evidence-based treatment exists — medication, therapy, and structured medical support — and most people who receive it improve significantly.

criteria.heading: What Is Alcohol Use Disorder?
criteria.description: The DSM-5 defines alcohol use disorder as a problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to significant impairment or distress, with at least 2 of the following occurring within a 12-month period:

items.label: Drinking more than intended
items.description: Often drinking more or for longer than you planned to.

items.label: Failed attempts to cut back
items.description: Wanting to cut down or control drinking but being unable to.

items.label: Significant time spent
items.description: Spending a lot of time obtaining alcohol, drinking, or recovering from its effects.

items.label: Cravings
items.description: A strong desire or urge to drink.

items.label: Failure to meet obligations
items.description: Drinking interferes with work, school, or home responsibilities.

items.label: Continued use despite problems
items.description: Continuing to drink even though it's causing relationship, legal, or health problems.

items.label: Giving up activities
items.description: Cutting back on or giving up social, occupational, or recreational activities because of drinking.

items.label: Drinking in dangerous situations
items.description: Drinking while driving, operating machinery, or in other risky situations.

items.label: Tolerance
items.description: Needing more alcohol to get the same effect, or feeling less effect with the same amount.

items.label: Withdrawal
items.description: Experiencing withdrawal symptoms — sweating, shaking, anxiety, nausea — when cutting back or stopping.

criteria.note: 2–3 criteria indicate mild AUD; 4–5 moderate; 6+ severe. Severity does not determine whether you deserve treatment — any level can cause significant harm and respond well to treatment. Physical dependence, indicated by tolerance and withdrawal, places you at medical risk if you stop abruptly without support.

howItFeels.heading: What Alcohol Use Disorder Actually Looks Like
paragraphs: Alcohol acts primarily on two receptor systems in the brain: GABA, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, and NMDA, the main excitatory one. Alcohol enhances GABA — producing sedation and relief — while suppressing NMDA. The brain is adaptive: with chronic heavy use, it compensates by downregulating GABA receptors and upregulating NMDA receptors, attempting to maintain balance in a system that has been chemically shifted. This process is physical dependence. It is not weakness. It is what the brain does when its chemistry is altered repeatedly over time. Once it has occurred, the body requires alcohol to feel normal — and stopping abruptly forces a reckoning with the compensatory changes that have built up.

When heavy, chronic use stops, the sedating effect of alcohol is removed but the neurological adaptations remain. Withdrawal begins within 6 to 12 hours of the last drink. Early symptoms — anxiety, sweating, tremor, elevated heart rate, nausea, insomnia — reflect an overactivated nervous system no longer held in check. Between 24 and 48 hours, the risk of withdrawal seizures peaks. These are generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and they can occur even in people with no prior seizure history. Between 48 and 96 hours, a subset of people will develop delirium tremens: severe confusion, agitation, fever, visual and tactile hallucinations, and dangerous swings in blood pressure and heart rate. Without treatment, delirium tremens carries meaningful mortality risk. With medically managed detox, outcomes are far better — but this is why stopping heavy, chronic drinking without medical supervision can be life-threatening.

Each episode of withdrawal can make the next one more severe — a process called kindling. With repeated cycles of heavy use and withdrawal, the brain's threshold for seizure activity lowers. Someone who has detoxed several times may experience seizures in a subsequent withdrawal that were absent in earlier ones, even with similar drinking patterns. Kindling is not universal, but it is a real and well-documented phenomenon, and it is one of the reasons that cycling in and out of unsupported detox is not a neutral activity. The medical risk of withdrawal compounds over time.

Alcohol use disorder rarely looks the way people imagine. Many people with AUD are employed, functional, and managing — for a time. Tolerance is often the clearest early signal: what was two drinks becomes four, then six, then the starting point of the evening. Blackouts — periods of use during which no new memories form — become more frequent. People begin drinking earlier in the day, or drinking specifically to stop the anxiety and tremor that starts before noon. Bottles are hidden; amounts are minimized in conversation. The morning drink — taken to quiet the shaking, not to get drunk — is the signature of significant physical dependence.

Alcohol is legal, culturally ubiquitous, and heavily marketed. This makes it uniquely difficult to see a drinking problem clearly. People compare themselves to a worse version they believe they haven't reached, or to someone who clearly has 'a real problem.' The shame associated with alcohol problems is often intense — sometimes more so than with illegal drugs — and it delays help-seeking by years. There is no threshold of severity required to deserve treatment. The question is not whether things are bad enough. The question is whether alcohol is causing harm and whether you want that to change.

treatmentSection.heading: How We Treat Alcohol Use Disorder
treatmentSection.intro: Effective, evidence-based treatment for AUD combines medical management of withdrawal, medication to reduce craving and relapse risk, and therapy to address the behavioral and psychological dimensions of the disorder. We tailor treatment to your situation — your level of physical dependence, your goals, and the other things going on in your life.

treatments.name: Outpatient Detoxification
treatments.description: For people with significant physical dependence, stopping abruptly without medical support is dangerous. Our outpatient detox protocol uses structured clinical assessment to evaluate withdrawal severity and determine the appropriate level of medication support. Most patients are managed with a tapered benzodiazepine protocol — which suppresses the overactive nervous system and substantially reduces the risk of seizures. Patients are monitored closely during the first several days. Outpatient detox is appropriate for mild to moderate withdrawal in a stable home environment; those with more severe dependence, a history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, or insufficient home support may require inpatient care, which we can help arrange.

treatments.name: Naltrexone
treatments.description: Naltrexone is one of the best-supported pharmacological treatments for AUD. It works by blocking opioid receptors that are part of the reward pathway making alcohol pleasurable — reducing both the craving to drink and the reinforcing effect if you do drink. It does not require full abstinence to be effective. Some people use it via the Sinclair Method, taking it before drinking and allowing alcohol to progressively lose its reinforcing effect over time. An extended-release injectable form (Vivitrol) is also available for those who prefer a monthly injection over a daily pill. Naltrexone is FDA-approved and dramatically underused relative to its effectiveness.

treatments.name: Acamprosate
treatments.description: Acamprosate works differently from naltrexone: rather than blocking reward, it stabilizes the glutamate and GABA imbalance that persists after alcohol withdrawal, reducing the dysphoria, anxiety, and restlessness that often drive relapse in early recovery. It works best for people committed to abstinence and is most effective when started after detox is complete. It is particularly useful for people whose main challenge is the uncomfortable post-acute withdrawal period — the weeks or months of low-grade discomfort that follow stopping.

treatments.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
treatments.description: CBT for AUD identifies the specific thoughts, feelings, and situations that trigger drinking and builds concrete skills for managing cravings, navigating high-risk situations, and responding differently to the emotional states that alcohol has been used to regulate. The evidence base for CBT in AUD is strong across severity levels, and the skills transfer — they don't stop working when treatment ends.

treatments.name: Motivational Interviewing
treatments.description: Most people with AUD are genuinely ambivalent about change — part of them wants to stop, and part of them doesn't. Motivational interviewing works with that ambivalence rather than against it. It helps you clarify your own values and goals, examine the discrepancy between where you are and where you want to be, and build your own reasons for change. It is not persuasion. It is structured conversation designed to help you get unstuck.

treatments.name: Family Therapy
treatments.description: Alcohol use disorder affects entire family systems — partners, parents, and children develop their own patterns of response that can inadvertently sustain the disorder. We work with families to understand the dynamics that have formed, set consistent and supportive expectations, improve communication, and create home conditions that support sustained recovery. Family involvement significantly improves long-term outcomes.

faqs.question: Do I have to want to quit completely, or can I try to moderate?
faqs.answer: Both are legitimate goals, and we'll work with whatever you're willing to try. Research supports both abstinence-based and moderation-oriented treatment approaches. That said, people with more severe alcohol use disorder typically have much better outcomes with abstinence. We'll have an honest conversation about what's likely to work for your situation.

faqs.question: Is it dangerous to stop drinking on my own?
faqs.answer: It can be. People who drink heavily every day, or who have a history of withdrawal seizures, should not stop abruptly without medical supervision. Alcohol withdrawal is one of the few withdrawal syndromes that can be life-threatening. If you're uncertain about the safety of stopping, call us — we'd rather help you be safe than have you take that risk alone.

faqs.question: What medications are used to treat alcohol use disorder?
faqs.answer: The most evidence-supported medications for alcohol use disorder are naltrexone, acamprosate, and disulfiram. Naltrexone reduces the pleasurable effects of alcohol and decreases craving — it doesn't require abstinence and has the strongest evidence base. Acamprosate reduces the discomfort of early abstinence. Disulfiram creates an aversive reaction to alcohol and works as a deterrent. We discuss these options and recommend based on your goals and situation.

faqs.question: Does naltrexone really work?
faqs.answer: Yes. Naltrexone is one of the best-supported pharmacological treatments for alcohol use disorder. It reduces the pleasurable effects of alcohol and decreases craving. It works best combined with therapy, and it doesn't require full abstinence to be effective — it's also used in the Sinclair Method, which some people find useful for moderation.

faqs.question: I've tried AA and it didn't work for me. What else is there?
faqs.answer: Quite a bit. AA works well for many people, but it's not the only evidence-supported path. CBT, motivational interviewing, SMART Recovery, medication, and combinations of these have solid research behind them. Not working in AA doesn't mean recovery isn't possible — it means you may need a different approach, and we can help identify what that looks like for you.

faqs.question: How long does outpatient alcohol treatment take?
faqs.answer: It varies considerably depending on severity and goals. CBT for alcohol use disorder typically runs 12–20 sessions. Medication management continues for as long as it is helpful — naltrexone is often continued for months to years in people at high risk of relapse. Unlike residential programs, outpatient treatment doesn't have a fixed discharge date. Progress is reviewed regularly and the plan adapts to where you are.

faqs.question: What if I'm also dealing with depression or anxiety?
faqs.answer: That's the norm, not the exception. Depression, anxiety, and alcohol use disorder co-occur at very high rates. We treat them together, because addressing only one usually means the other undermines your progress. Sometimes the mental health condition came first; sometimes alcohol use created or worsened it. Either way, integrated treatment works better than treating them separately.

faqs.question: Are there free support groups for alcohol use disorder?
faqs.answer: There are several, representing meaningfully different approaches. Alcoholics Anonymous (aa.org) is the foundational 12-step fellowship with meetings worldwide — the most widely available option. SMART Recovery (smartrecovery.org) is a secular, science-based alternative using CBT and motivational tools, with over 1,500 weekly meetings including online, and it works alongside medication. Moderation Management (moderation.org) is peer-led and non-judgmental for people whose goal is reducing rather than stopping drinking. LifeRing Secular Recovery (lifering.org) is another secular option with no higher-power requirement, well-suited to people who don't connect with 12-step. Women for Sobriety (womenforsobriety.org) is a women-only nonprofit program that addresses the emotional and self-esteem dimensions of recovery that are often most central for women — an underutilized resource. For family members and partners, Al-Anon (al-anon.org) has meetings worldwide and offers Alateen for younger family members. The r/stopdrinking community on Reddit has over 600,000 members with a daily check-in tradition and strong moderation.

resources.name: Alcoholics Anonymous
resources.description: The original 12-step fellowship for alcohol recovery — meetings worldwide, no dues or fees, open to anyone with a desire to stop drinking.

resources.name: SMART Recovery
resources.description: Science-based, secular alternative using CBT and motivational tools — 1,500+ meetings weekly including online. Compatible with medication-assisted treatment.

resources.name: Moderation Management
resources.description: Peer-led community for people who want to reduce their drinking rather than abstain entirely — non-judgmental meetings and online tools.

resources.name: LifeRing Secular Recovery
resources.description: Secular, present-focused mutual support — no higher-power requirement, convener-facilitated meetings online and in-person. A strong alternative for those who don't connect with 12-step.

resources.name: Women for Sobriety
resources.description: Women-only nonprofit founded 1975 — the 'New Life' program addresses the emotional and self-esteem dimensions of recovery that are often central for women.

resources.name: Al-Anon Family Groups
resources.description: 12-step program for family members and friends affected by someone's drinking — meetings worldwide, Alateen for younger family members.

resources.name: NIAAA Alcohol Treatment Navigator
resources.description: NIH guide to finding evidence-based alcohol treatment — explains what works, what to look for in a provider, and includes a treatment locator.

resources.name: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
resources.description: Call or text 988 — free, confidential, 24/7 crisis support for mental health emergencies and suicidal thoughts.
